#4855. CleanSpark weighs selling more Bitcoin than it mines to de-risk books

The Bitcoin miner sold 2,102 BTC while it produced just 1,708 BTC in the September quarter.

Bitcoin miner CleanSpark is considering selling more Bitcoin than it mines each quarter to reduce its treasury risk, according to chief financial officer Gary Vecchiarelli, potentially further drawing down its holdings, last valued at $806 million.

CleanSpark held 13,530 Bitcoin at the end of September after mining 1,708 Bitcoin and selling 2,102 Bitcoin during the quarter, according to Cointelegraph’s tally of the company’s monthly operating updates. It marks the first time since at least 2024 that the company ended the quarter with less Bitcoin than it began with.

During a Q4 earnings call on Tuesday, Vecchiarelli said CleanSpark already aims to sell virtually all of the Bitcoin it mines to cover day-to-day operating costs, and told an analyst that selling slightly more than it produces in a quarter was one way to reduce treasury risk.

“We see the selling of a small amount of Bitcoin in excess of the quarterly production to be one way of de-risking,” said Vecchiarelli.

“But again, we are going to be sensitive and very reactionary to markets, and we are going to use that capital to make sure that we prevent dilution or bringing additional debt just to grow the company,” he said.

The remarks came as CleanSpark recorded a $987 million net loss for the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, compared with a net income of $364 million a year earlier. The company attributed two-thirds of the swing to noncash adjustments in the value of its Bitcoin holdings, as Bitcoin’s price fell from about $114,100 to $83,600 over the fiscal year.

Related: Trump-linked American Bitcoin secures $150M credit line from FalconX

CleanSpark also said it sold an undisclosed amount of Bitcoin since September to raise cash for expected acquisitions, as Vecchiarelli said it continues to view its Bitcoin holdings as “a liquid source of non-dilutive capital.”

CleanSpark also cut about 25,000 machines from its Bitcoin mining fleet in the September quarter, bringing the number in operation to about 200,000.

Vecchiarelli said the reduction improved energy efficiency to 14.8 joules per terahash from 15.8 in the previous quarter, which he said should help CleanSpark stay profitable if mining conditions deteriorate ahead of the 2028 Bitcoin halving.

“Going forward, in terms of hash rate, that will probably fluctuate, but we will continue to mine so as long as it’s profitable.”

In Sandersville, Georgia, CleanSpark said its first AI data hall remains on track for the fourth quarter of 2027. CleanSpark said it expects to start unplugging miners at the site in late 2027 as the data center comes online, then decide whether to relocate or sell them.

CleanSpark shares dropped 7.5% on Tuesday ahead of the earnings release to $5.12 and are down 2.25% in after-hours trading.

The company recorded $576.5 million in total revenue in the full year, down 25% from the previous fiscal year. Adjusted EBITDA came in at a loss of $304.2 million for the year.

London’s High Court entered the judgment on Nov. 20 against Vivek Kumar Sen and Zamyang Sherpa after neither man filed an acknowledgment of service or a defence, with Master Teverson ruling in favor of X without a trial.

A default judgment means the court entered the order because the defendants failed to engage, not because the allegations were tested and proven. Either defendant can apply within seven days of being served to have the order varied or set aside.

The case dates to a claim issued Sept. 21, when X sued the pair and unidentified accomplices for allegedly operating a coordinated bot army to inflate engagement and siphon money from its Creator Revenue Sharing program.

Crucially, the judgment awards no money yet. Because X sued for “an unspecified sum,” the order states the amount of damages and interest will be decided later at a separate Disposal Hearing.

X has estimated the improperly obtained revenue at no less than £207,384 (about $271,000) and said it is seeking at least £75,000 ($98,000) more in investigation and remediation costs. Those are the company’s claimed figures, not sums the court has granted.

X General Counsel James Burnham announced the ruling, writing that the company had “sued people who abused Creator Revenue Sharing by operating a network of accounts to manipulate engagement” and that the court had now entered judgment against two of them.

“We aren’t kidding around,” he added. “Fraudsters worldwide: Do not mess with X.” Musk reposted the statement with his own terse endorsement.

Even once damages are set, recovering the money is a separate matter that depends on whatever assets Sen and Sherpa hold.

The case reflects the broader strain of the “engagement economy,” where platforms paying creators based on activity have become targets for coordinated manipulation.

X retired Creator Revenue Sharing, which launched in 2023 and paid out based on engagement, on Sept. 7, replacing it the next day with Original Content Rewards, a system it says emphasizes original material over raw engagement volume, a shift partly aimed at the kind of gaming alleged here.

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 25, 2026

The FCC even brought a bit of science fiction into its announcement, suggesting the project could bring humanity closer to becoming a Kardashev Type II civilization—a hypothetical society capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its star.

SpaceX originally submitted its proposal in January, with the FCC opening a review in February, shortly after Musk folded his AI startup xAI, the developer of Grok, into SpaceX.

Unlike Starlink satellites, which primarily provide internet connectivity, Starmind satellites would perform computations themselves, exchanging information through laser communications. The authorization also allows SpaceX to use radio frequencies as a backup for communications and emergency satellite controls.

Electricity has become one of the biggest bottlenecks in the AI industry. Companies can spend billions of dollars building data centers and buying chips, only to find that local power grids cannot supply enough electricity to run them.

Satellites operating in certain orbits can receive sunlight almost continuously, making solar panels up to eight times more productive than their counterparts on Earth, according to Google research.

Google is pursuing a similar initiative called Project Suncatcher. The company launched its first prototype in October and selected Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’ space company, for another mission scheduled for 2029.

Keeping computers cool in space, despite its reputation for being extremely cold, is surprisingly difficult. The vacuum prevents heat from dissipating through air, meaning satellites need radiators to expel the heat generated by AI chips, which must also withstand exposure to cosmic radiation.

There are environmental concerns, too. The Center for Space Environmentalism warned in September that manufacturing, deploying and eventually deorbiting a constellation of this size could contribute significantly to atmospheric pollution. The FCC said Starmind complies with its orbital debris regulations.

Getting permission to launch a million satellites and actually putting them in orbit are two very different things. During an investment conference earlier this month, Musk estimated that the first Starmind computers could launch in the third quarter of 2027.

SpaceX’s securities disclosures have previously warned investors that its orbital computing business has yet to demonstrate commercial viability and could ultimately prove unsuccessful.

#4846. Nvidia to Pay $290 Million to Settle Long-Running Crypto Mining Revenue Lawsuit

Nvidia to Pay $290 Million to Settle Long-Running Crypto Mining Revenue Lawsuit

Nvidia has agreed to pay $290 million to settle a shareholder lawsuit dating back to 2018, resolving long-running claims that the chipmaker misled investors about how much of its soaring gaming revenue was actually driven by cryptocurrency miners.

According to a court filing Tuesday, the proposed cash settlement would close a case rooted in the 2017-2018 crypto boom, when miners snapped up Nvidia’s GeForce GPUs to mint coins, with the sales booked as gaming revenue.

As Decrypt reported, shareholders alleged Nvidia downplayed its dependence on that volatile mining demand, leaving investors blindsided when the boom collapsed.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

In November 2018, the company cut its quarterly revenue forecast as mining demand evaporated, and its stock tumbled roughly 28% over the following two trading sessions.

The settlement covers investors who bought Nvidia stock between Aug. 10, 2017, and Nov. 15, 2018. An analysis commissioned by the plaintiffs estimated Nvidia had understated its crypto-related GPU sales by about $1.1 billion over that stretch.

The company has consistently denied wrongdoing, arguing it could not reliably quantify how much of its gaming revenue stemmed from mining, and it is not admitting liability as part of the deal.

The case has taken a winding, years-long path through the courts. A district court dismissed the suit in March 2021 for failure to adequately allege the executives knew they were misleading investors. A federal appeals court then partly revived it in 2023, keeping the claims alive against Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang while dismissing those against two other executives, including Colette Kress, the finance chief who briefly served as interim CEO during Huang’s recent ouster.

The dispute then reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which heard arguments before dismissing the appeal in December 2024 without ruling on the merits. The district court certified the class in March 2026, and the $290 million figure emerged from mediation led by former federal judge Layn Phillips, whose recommendation both sides accepted in September.

The sum is modest for a company whose market value has swelled into the trillions on the AI boom.

Plaintiffs’ damages expert pegged the maximum the class could have won at trial at about $2.06 billion, meaning the settlement represents roughly 14% of those potential damages, a figure the plaintiffs’ lawyers note compares favorably with typical securities-case recoveries.

Those attorneys said they plan to seek up to 21.4% of the fund, or about $62 million, in legal fees, which they stressed sits below the Ninth Circuit’s 25% benchmark.

The settlement still requires court approval. Under the plaintiffs’ proposed schedule, the court would first decide whether to grant preliminary approval and send notice to affected shareholders, with a final settlement hearing to follow about 130 days later.

Notably, the deal is unrelated to the separate, far more recent turmoil around Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang, whose brief ouster and reinstatement this month over a spy-tinged scandal rattled markets.

For Nvidia, the agreement finally draws a line under one of the last major legal hangovers from crypto’s last great mining frenzy.

A fintech or technology company could still hold a larger stake than any individual bank.

The proposal follows months of regulatory disagreements. The Bank of Korea has advocated for bank-led issuance, citing monetary policy and financial stability risks, while the FSC previously favored allowing nonbank companies to issue stablecoins.

If the Banking Act’s 15% limit on a bank’s stake in a nonfinancial company applies to stablecoin issuers, at least four banks would need to join each consortium to secure a majority, according to Tiger Research.

Vincent Chok, founder and CEO of First Digital, whose subsidiary issues the FDUSD stablecoin, told Cointelegraph that bank-majority consortiums could give won-denominated stablecoins credibility at launch, while fintech participation could help preserve innovation.

“Beyond who issues, Korea’s ability to capture the wider economic activity around stablecoins will rest on efficient on- and off-ramps and rails connecting KRW with global dollar liquidity,” Chok said.

South Korean financial and technology companies have already started exploring these opportunities. In May, KB Financial Group completed a won-denominated stablecoin pilot covering merchant payments and cross-border remittances. In July, Viva Republica, which operates the Toss payments app, partnered with Optimism and Sunnyside Labs to test stablecoin-based payments for financial institutions.

Related: How South Korea’s proposed 20% cap could change who runs Upbit

The bill still needs to pass the National Assembly before proceeding to presidential promulgation. Tiger Research said the legislation is expected to take effect one year after promulgation, while key details, including shareholder requirements for stablecoin consortiums, remain subject to subsequent enforcement decrees.

#4844. What Is Artex? The AI Hacking Tool Linked to the US Spy Agency Breach

What Is Artex? The AI Hacking Tool Linked to the US Spy Agency Breach

The AI tool reportedly used to breach a system shared by three U.S. intelligence agencies is already part of the arsenal of at least six hacking groups tracked by Microsoft, according to research published Wednesday.

Artex, a framework originally developed to help cybersecurity professionals find security flaws, was reportedly involved in an intrusion affecting the CIA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

The compromised system analyzes information collected from publicly available sources, according to the Associated Press. The identity of the hackers and the AI model they used remain unconfirmed.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

In one analysis, Microsoft's threat intelligence team identified both financially motivated criminals and state-sponsored groups using the software, including Salt Typhoon, Crystal Typhoon, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Storm-0940, and Storm-3358. Microsoft did not attribute the spy agency breach to any of them.

“ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques,” Microsoft wrote.

The CIA intrusion, disclosed Tuesday, affected a shared intelligence analysis system that draws on sources such as social media, commercial satellite imagery, and data brokers. A source told Nextgov/FCW that the breach had been resolved and classified systems were unaffected. What information, if any, was stolen remains unclear, though such an intrusion could expose analysts' investigative priorities.

The NSA suffered a similar breach exposing unclassified information, according to the New York Times. Prior, the NSA's classified internal communications network was restored on November 20 after several days of disruption. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton attributed the outage to software patching rather than a cyberattack. The Donald Trump administration has denied that the recent outages were part of a coordinated attack.

Separately, the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, a database used by law enforcement agencies nationwide that contains criminal histories, records of missing persons, fugitives, and stolen property. Investigators have not publicly established the extent of the intrusion or whether records were stolen.

Artex is not an AI model like ChatGPT's GPT or Anthropic's Claude. It is an agentic harness, a piece of software that lets language models interact with other programs and perform tasks rather than simply generate text.

A developer known as Autumn-27 published the project on GitHub in July. Written in Go, it was designed for penetration testing, the practice of attempting to break into computer systems with the owner's permission to identify security weaknesses.

The framework divides work among specialized AI agents responsible for planning, carrying out assessments, and reporting their results, according to Google's threat intelligence team. A shared record of findings helps the agents retain context and coordinate their work over lengthy assignments.

The underlying AI is interchangeable. Microsoft says Artex can use commercial and open-weight models, which means the framework is not necessarily subject to the safety policies of any one AI company.

Microsoft says that under certain conditions Artex can obtain lasting access with elevated permissions in minutes, rather than requiring someone to oversee each stage of an operation.

Artex attracted international attention in October after attacks on South Korean financial institutions. A November 13 FBI advisory linked the campaign to the theft of personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 people.

Autumn-27 removed the original repository in October following reports of criminal abuse. By early November, researchers had counted more than 1,600 publicly exposed Artex installations, according to the FBI, though that does not mean all were operated by criminals.

Removing an open-source repository does not erase the copies others have downloaded or the independent versions they have created. Microsoft says that this month Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of Artex and began selling access to a commercial offering called Artex Pro.

The problem is not unique to Artex. Security researchers have long released tools that criminals later repurposed, but AI reduces the amount of manual work involved in running them.

The FBI has tracked Artex-related activity across 10 industries since August, including government, defense, finance, and technology.

On November 13, Amazon researchers described campaigns believed to involve Artex, including attempts to steal AI service credentials and circumvent identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges using deepfakes.

The identity verification system rejected every synthetic video attempt documented by the agents. Amazon also cautioned that it could not independently verify all the outcomes the agents claimed to have achieved.

As Decrypt reported last year, Anthropic said suspected Chinese state-sponsored hackers had already used Claude to automate 80% to 90% of the tactical work in a cyberespionage campaign targeting roughly 30 organizations.

Smaller criminal groups now have access to software that handles some of the coordination previously left to experienced hackers. They still need vulnerable targets, and defenders can still stop them.

Britain's National Cyber Security Centre said Tuesday that it had seen a sharp increase in AI-assisted attacks since September, with criminals exploiting familiar problems such as poorly secured accounts and misconfigured software.

For organizations defending themselves, the immediate priority remains fixing those weaknesses, reducing the number of publicly exposed systems, and improving detection. Britain's cybersecurity agency says today's agentic frameworks are relatively noisy, giving defenders a chance to spot them, though future versions may be harder to detect.

#4840. Stablecoin redemptions hit $12B in 30 days, echoing 2022 bear market

Crypto research firm Kaiko said the cash-out was smaller than in 2022 and has slowed, with stablecoin supply down just 0.4% since Nov. 13.

Net redemptions across the 11 stablecoins tracked by crypto research firm Kaiko reached about $12 billion in the 30 days to Nov. 13, echoing a pattern analysts saw during the 2022 bear market.

Tether’s USDt (USDT) and Circle’s USDC (USDC), the two largest stablecoins, each ended the period with about 4% fewer tokens in circulation. Since Nov. 13, total stablecoin supply has fallen just 0.4%, while USDC supply has edged higher.

“The contraction looks like capital leaving crypto rather than rotating within it,” Kaiko analyst Andrew Yang told Cointelegraph.

Yang said that the redemptions left traders with fewer stablecoins on hand to buy crypto.

The cash-out coincided with outflows from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds and a shift in expectations toward tighter Federal Reserve policy.

Daily trading volume in USDT pairs was about half its 2025 average over the past month, according to Kaiko. Bitcoin (BTC) market makers continued to post orders close to the market price.

The dollar value of orders to buy or sell Bitcoin within 1% of its market price fell about 15% over the past month. Measured in Bitcoin, those orders were 9% larger in aggregate, Yang said.

Related: Stablecoin supply falls $14.2B in biggest 30-day drop since June 2022

Nearly 90% of the 30-day decline in stablecoin supply came from Ethereum, a major hub for exchanges and decentralized finance. On Tron, a network more commonly used for payments, stablecoin supply fell just 1.4%, according to Kaiko.

Onchain transfers of USDT and USDC have averaged about $157 billion a day so far this quarter. That’s above the 2025 daily average of $130 billion, though below the pace in the fourth quarter of last year, Kaiko said.

During the 2022–2023 bear market, rising interest rates and falling crypto prices drove months of redemptions from fiat-backed stablecoins, Yang said. He described the current pullback as much smaller and pointed to a more recent comparison. Stablecoin supply fell from mid-May into June this year before stabilizing in August.

For USDT, the latest decline is the largest since 2022, said Julio Moreno, head of research at blockchain analytics firm CryptoQuant. Its market capitalization has fallen $9 billion over the past 60 days, a drop Moreno linked to a broader retreat from risk assets, including stocks and commodities.

Moreno tracks USDT supply as a measure of the funds available for trading. Exchanges hold 51% of the USDT circulating on Ethereum, he told Cointelegraph.

USDT supply was also shrinking when Bitcoin bottomed in November 2022, Moreno said.

He said stablecoin supply would have to grow again “in order for liquidity to improve and the market to recover.”

#4839. Another Bitcoin Mining Firm Flags 'Hashrate Hijacking' Attacks That Reroute Rewards

Another Bitcoin Mining Firm Flags 'Hashrate Hijacking' Attacks That Reroute Rewards

For the second time in weeks, a major Bitcoin mining firm has warned that attackers are siphoning mining rewards by hijacking the internet connections between miners and their pools, a sign that a long-dormant weakness in mining’s plumbing is now being exploited at scale.

Mining software firm Braiins said Wednesday that an attacker struck more than a thousand mining sites in a single second on Nov. 20, rerouting their connections to an impostor pool.

It follows a similar incident just last week, when mining-services firm Luxor reported that hackers had redirected miner rewards, which it tied to AI-assisted attacks.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The two firms described somewhat different mechanisms, but the effect was the same: hashrate quietly diverted away from the miners who produced it.

In its security alert, Braiins stressed the attacker didn’t need to break into any miner or into Braiins Pool itself. Instead, they exploited a long-standing flaw in Stratum V1, the unencrypted, plain-text protocol that carries work between miners and pools and offers no way to verify that the server on the other end is the real pool.

By rerouting traffic, the attacker impersonated the pool, fed miners legitimate-looking jobs, and pocketed the resulting shares under their own account at a separate pool.

The scheme hinged on manipulating the Border Gateway Protocol, or BGP, the trust-based system that tells networks where to route internet traffic. The attacker announced a narrower, more specific block of addresses that included a pool’s Stratum endpoint, causing networks that failed to validate the route to funnel miners’ connections to the impostor.

Hijacked machines kept hashing at full power while their pool dashboards showed zero hashrate, making the theft nearly invisible on-site.

Braiins traced episodes starting in early November across Latin America, mostly Brazil and Argentina, before a larger Nov. 20 wave hit mostly European miners, diverting between 0.6 and 1.9 exahashes per second at a time. The firm characterized the short, escalating bursts as the attacker “testing the waters,” noting the diverted hashrate grew more than tenfold in two weeks.

The technique isn’t new. Braiins noted that Dell SecureWorks documented the same routing trick stealing roughly $83,000 in mining rewards back in 2014, and the firm has warned about “hashrate hijacking” since 2020 as a reason to adopt the encrypted Stratum V2 protocol.

For years, the industry treated it as rare enough to tolerate; now, two firms in a matter of weeks have flagged it hitting miners in the wild.

Braiins urged the whole industry to act, recommending miners move to Stratum V2 or Stratum V1 over TLS with certificate verification, strip out plain-text backup connections, and push network operators to validate routes. It also released a free proxy tool for miners that can’t upgrade.

Any miner still on plain Stratum V1, the firm said, “is a target, on any pool.”

#4837. French Senate rejects 100K euro crypto wallet disclosure requirement

Senators also rejected stablecoin-swap and crypto exit-tax proposals, while the 2027 budget remains under parliamentary consideration.

The French Senate rejected proposals Tuesday that would have required taxpayers to declare self-custodied crypto holdings worth at least 100,000 euros (about $109,600) to tax authorities.

Senators voted down identical amendments from Pascal Savoldelli and Anne-Sophie Romagny during debate on the 2027 budget. The requirement would have applied when the combined value of crypto held in wallets outside a service provider reached at least 100,000 euros on Dec. 31.

The reporting requirement was initially adopted by the National Assembly on Nov. 3, but fell when lawmakers rejected the budget’s entire revenue section on Nov. 4.

Budget Minister David Amiel opposed the wallet-reporting amendments, saying they would not enable authorities to track how crypto is used, particularly in money laundering or tax fraud. The Senate’s finance committee followed the government’s recommendation to reject them.

Requiring a declaration of wallet holdings without a taxable event would amount to “placing a blanket suspicion on good-faith users,” Faustine Fleuret, global head of public affairs at lending protocol Morpho, told Cointelegraph.

She said that self-custodial wallet reporting would create “unequal treatment” compared to other assets like jewelry or fine art, “whose mere holding is not subject to a reporting obligation in the absence of a taxable transaction.”

Related: Lagarde warns Europe could miss chance to unify tokenized markets

The Senate also rejected another amendment from Savoldelli that would have taxed gains on crypto conversions into stablecoins classified as electronic-money tokens under EU rules. It would have applied from Jan. 1, 2027.

The Assembly adopted a similar amendment from MP Nicolas Sansu on Oct. 16, but that measure also fell when the Assembly rejected the revenue section. Savoldelli reintroduced the proposal on Nov. 19 before Tuesday’s rejection.

A proposal to extend France’s exit tax to unrealized crypto gains when qualifying taxpayers moved their tax residence abroad also failed. The Assembly rejected similar proposals on Oct. 30.

Another crypto-related amendment remains pending. Senator Thomas Dossus’s amendment would raise a proposed fine for refusing tax authorities’ information requests from 10,000 euros to 50,000 euros per request. It would cover financial institutions, crypto service providers and platform operators.

The Senate is scheduled to complete debate and vote on the budget’s revenue section Saturday, with Sunday available if needed.

A Senate vote on the full budget is scheduled for Dec. 9. The rejected crypto measures are absent from the text as it stands, but the budget still faces further negotiations before final adoption.

#4834. The 1Password Breach Didn’t Touch Your Vault. The Phishing Emails Might

The 1Password Breach Didn’t Touch Your Vault. The Phishing Emails Might

Password manager 1Password has disclosed a security breach in which an attacker accessed some of its backend systems and copied customer account information, though the company says the vaults where users store their passwords and other secrets were never touched.

In a disclosure published Tuesday, the Toronto-based firm said it began investigating on Nov. 19 after detecting that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The intruder used that access to reach

1Password’s source code and push malicious code to backend services, which then downloaded administrative data on a subset of customers. At no point, the company said, were vault contents accessible to the attacker.

Here’s what was taken, according to 1Password: customer names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys (which are public by design), certain protocol parameters that can’t be used to access an account, and non-secret internal metadata.

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to the company’s software build systems, which hold some infrastructure credentials. 1Password said it has rotated all credentials that may have been exposed.

Crucially for users, the breach did not expose the data that actually matters: your vaults, the items inside them, the keys that protect them, or your account recovery keys.

1Password’s design means it never stores your account password or Secret Key, so an attacker who gets into its servers still can’t decrypt your vault. The company stressed there’s nothing you need to change in your account, and its apps and browser extensions are working normally.

What users should do, for now, comes down to what is generally good advice at all times: watch out for phishing emails, because they’re surely coming.

Because names and email addresses were exposed, affected users are prime targets for scam emails impersonating 1Password, particularly fake account-recovery or invitation requests.

The company urged caution with any unexpected message mentioning 1Password, and reiterated that it will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key, which you should only ever enter in the official app or on the official site after opening it yourself.

One wrinkle involves emailed invitation and recovery links, which contain a token. 1Password said a small number of users in that state were notified directly; as a precaution, it lengthened the verification codes in those emails from six digits to ten alphanumeric characters to make guessing them impractical.

The incident echoes a run of breaches hitting companies that hold users’ most sensitive data, a pattern that has emerged this year as attackers increasingly target third-party systems and developer accounts rather than the encryption itself.

Realized price represents the average price at which each Bitcoin last moved onchain. When the spot price falls below this level, currently around $53,200, holders are collectively sitting on an unrealized loss.

During prior bear markets, Bitcoin fell through its realized price before establishing its next long-term floor.

During Bitcoin’s last bear market in 2022, price spent 180 days below realized price before reclaiming it in January 2023. The record for time spent below investors’ aggregate cost basis is 301 days across 2014 and 2015, per calculations from Bitfinex Alpha, the research arm of crypto exchange Bitfinex.

Applying previous declines below realized price to today’s level would put Bitcoin at about $45,000 in a repeat of the March 2020 crash, or around $41,000 and $37,000 using the 2022 and 2018 bear-market lows, respectively.

“Should this time not be different after all, we would expect price to go lower and close below the Realized Price, which is a little over 10% away,” Glassnode added.

The HKMA’s new platform supports settlement in multiple currencies and handles debt issuance, interest payments and repayment at maturity.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) launched a platform Wednesday that supports round-the-clock settlement of tokenized debt securities in multiple currencies.

The CMU Digital Asset Platform, developed and operated by CMU OmniClear Limited on behalf of the HKMA, uses cash tokens for payment and connects with conventional payment systems and central bank digital currencies.

Its onchain delivery-versus-payment model ensures that the securities and corresponding payment transfer together, or neither transfer occurs. This means the buyer receives the securities only if the seller receives payment.

The platform also handles issuance, interest payments and repayment at maturity, and supports the tokenization of existing debt securities. The HKMA said it aims to improve settlement efficiency and reduce operational costs.

The launch follows a separate expansion of Hong Kong’s digital payment infrastructure. On Nov. 2, the HKMA upgraded its Project Ensemble pilot to support 24/7 interbank settlement of tokenized deposit transactions using tokenized central bank money.

The pilot phase launched in November 2025 and initially used Hong Kong’s conventional real-time gross settlement system. Its applications have included corporate treasury management and transactions involving tokenized money market funds.

Ukraine’s parliament passed a bill Wednesday to regulate the cryptocurrency market and tax individuals’ profits from digital asset transactions.

Individuals would generally pay an 18% personal income tax and a 5% military levy on their net annual crypto profits. Crypto-to-crypto swaps would be exempt, and investors could carry forward losses to offset future crypto gains, Ukraine’s state news agency Ukrinform reported.

Investors who bought crypto before the rules take effect could opt for a lower income tax rate if they sell those holdings for fiat currency by the end of 2028. Under that option, the 5% income tax and 5% military levy would both apply to the full sale proceeds.

The National Bank of Ukraine would share oversight of the crypto market with the country’s National Securities and Stock Market Commission. The central bank would oversee issuers of stablecoins pegged to a single official currency.

The bill would also set rules for admitting foreign tokens that can function as electronic money to the Ukrainian market, central bank Governor Andriy Pyshnyy said.

#4818. Here’s what happened in crypto today

Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.

Today in crypto, stablecoin redemptions echoed a pattern seen during the 2022 bear market, CleanSpark’s chief financial officer said the company could consider selling more Bitcoin than it mines to reduce treasury risk and Coinkite disclosed how a software error left Coldcard users’ Bitcoin recovery phrases vulnerable to hackers.

Net redemptions across the 11 stablecoins tracked by crypto research firm Kaiko reached about $12 billion in the 30 days to Nov. 13, echoing a pattern analysts saw during the 2022 bear market.

Tether’s USDt (USDT$) and Circle’s USDC (USDC), the two largest stablecoins, each ended the period with about 4% fewer tokens in circulation. Since Nov. 13, total stablecoin supply has fallen just 0.4%, while USDC supply has edged higher.

“The contraction looks like capital leaving crypto rather than rotating within it,” Kaiko analyst Andrew Yang told Cointelegraph.

Yang said that the redemptions left traders with fewer stablecoins on hand to buy crypto.

The cash-out coincided with outflows from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds and a shift in expectations toward tighter Federal Reserve policy.

Bitcoin miner CleanSpark is considering selling more Bitcoin than it mines each quarter to reduce its treasury risk, according to chief financial officer Gary Vecchiarelli, potentially further drawing down its holdings, last valued at $806 million.

CleanSpark held 13,530 Bitcoin at the end of September after mining 1,708 Bitcoin and selling 2,102 Bitcoin during the quarter, according to Cointelegraph’s tally of the company’s monthly operating updates. It marks the first time since at least 2024 that the company ended the quarter with less Bitcoin than it began with.

During a Q4 earnings call on Tuesday, Vecchiarelli said CleanSpark already aims to sell virtually all of the Bitcoin it mines to cover day-to-day operating costs, and told an analyst that selling slightly more than it produces in a quarter was one way to reduce treasury risk.

“We see the selling of a small amount of Bitcoin in excess of the quarterly production to be one way of de-risking,” said Vecchiarelli.

“But again, we are going to be sensitive and very reactionary to markets, and we are going to use that capital to make sure that we prevent dilution or bringing additional debt just to grow the company,” he said.

The remarks came as CleanSpark recorded a $987 million net loss for the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, compared with a net income of $364 million a year earlier. The company attributed two-thirds of the swing to noncash adjustments in the value of its Bitcoin holdings, as Bitcoin’s price fell from about $114,100 to $83,600 over the fiscal year.

Bitcoin hardware wallet maker Coinkite has detailed how a security flaw in its Coldcard devices went undetected for more than five years despite several independent security reviews, including those using artificial intelligence (AI).

In a Nov. 23 postmortem report, Coinkite said that while its security checks confirmed the wallets had the correct system for generating secure recovery phrases, the company never verified whether the wallets were actually using it. As a result, a software error caused the wallets to use a weaker system instead, making the recovery phrases easier for hackers to guess.

A Bitcoin hardware wallet is a physical device that stores private keys offline, while a recovery phrase is a series of words that allows users to restore access to their funds if the device is lost or damaged.

Coinkite said at least 15 independent security reviews and research efforts failed to catch the flaw before the thefts began. It added that the weaker system went undetected because the recovery phrases looked normal and could still pass some security tests.

The flaw allowed hackers to steal at least 1,789 Bitcoin (BTC), worth around $114.7 million at the time of the thefts, Galaxy Research reported in August. Coinkite said it fixed the flaw on July 31 and introduced further security measures in August.

#4815. Ex-FTX COO calls out Netflix over CZ’s ‘Asian mafia’ portrayal

Constance Waing said Netflix used racist stereotypes in its portrayal of CZ and misrepresented life at FTX before the exchange’s collapse.

Former FTX chief operating officer Constance Waing called Netflix’s portrayal of Binance founder Changpeng Zhao in The Altruists racist, saying it relied on Asian mafia stereotypes.

“It’s very racist,” Waing told Cointelegraph during Wednesday’s episode of the Chain Reaction show on X Spaces.

Waing took issue with a scene in which FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried and former Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison enter through a back door to meet Zhao, who is also known as “CZ.” She said it portrayed Zhao as an Asian mafia figure “trying to get these two innocent people into something bad.”

The Altruists, which premiered Thursday, is a dramatization of the rise and fall of Bankman-Fried’s crypto empire. Once considered crypto’s golden boy, Bankman-Fried presided over FTX until its collapse in November 2022, when a run on customer deposits exposed a multibillion-dollar shortfall.

In the fourth episode, Zhao’s character urges Bankman-Fried and Ellison to give Alameda Research advance access to FTX customer orders so it can trade ahead of them.

The scene drew criticism from Zhao himself, who called it “insane” and questioned how it would shape public perception in an X post.

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin also criticized the scene for exaggerating Zhao’s accent and questioned whether the portrayal was racist.

Series creator Graham Moore identified the scene as fiction in a Friday essay for Vulture, writing that “there’s no evidence that CZ ever specifically pressured FTX to front-run.”

Related: Sam Bankman-Fried wrote to actor portraying him in Netflix series

Waing watched the series with former FTX and Alameda colleagues and concluded that the show is “completely made up.” She disputed its portrayal of office parties, executive relationships and her own response to problems at the exchange.

Many FTX employees kept all their money on the exchange before its collapse, according to Waing. One employee in Hong Kong could not afford a ticket home, so someone else had to buy it for him.

Waing stayed in the Bahamas after FTX collapsed to seek answers from Bankman-Fried.

“The only thing Sam told me was ‘I’m sorry, I fucked up,’” Waing said, recalling their last conversation before his extradition to the US.

She said she received no explanation beyond what Bankman-Fried said in public interviews and has not spoken to him or Ellison since that period.

Bankman-Fried was convicted on seven fraud and conspiracy counts and sentenced to 25 years in prison in March 2024. Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 and testified against Bankman-Fried. She received a two-year prison sentence in September 2024.

#4812. FCC authorizes SpaceX to deploy 1M satellites for orbital AI data centers

The planned Starmind constellation will process data in orbit for use on Earth, as demand for artificial intelligence computing power continues to grow.

The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has authorized Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites as part of a planned network of orbital data centers, in what the agency described as a historic first.

According to a Wednesday FCC announcement, the satellite constellation, dubbed “Starmind,” is designed to provide orbital computing infrastructure to meet growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI), processing large amounts of data for use on Earth.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the authorization opens a new frontier for computing infrastructure, as SpaceX and other companies seek to move data processing capacity beyond Earth. The agency said it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals.

The Starmind satellites will communicate with one another using optical links, with radio frequencies serving as a backup for communications and emergency operations. The FCC said the system complies with its orbital debris rules.

The FCC did not specify a deployment timeline or estimated cost for the Starmind constellation.

SpaceX first applied for permission to launch up to 1 million orbital data center satellites on Jan. 30, with the FCC opening the proposal to public comment on Feb. 4.

Just three days after submitting its application, the company completed its acquisition of Musk’s AI company xAI, the developer of the Grok chatbot, bringing its space and AI businesses under one umbrella.

However, the proposal drew opposition from Amazon Leo, Amazon’s satellite internet business, which petitioned the FCC in March to reject the application, citing insufficient details about satellite designs, orbital configurations and collision prevention measures.

SpaceX pushed back, arguing that its use of optical communications would limit interference with competing satellite networks. Ahead of its initial public offering (IPO) in June, the company disclosed that satellite deployment could begin as early as 2028.

SpaceX’s launch milestones and operational statistics as of March 31, 2026. Source: SpaceX S-1 filing

In a video released during the IPO process, Musk argued that harnessing solar energy in space “avoids the need to build massive power plants on Earth” and could simplify the cooling of computing infrastructure.

SpaceX has also enlisted Nvidia in the development of its orbital computing infrastructure. In August, the chipmaker announced that the first-generation Starmind satellite would use a modified version of its Vera Rubin NVL72 computing system.

The FCC’s authorization comes amid mounting public opposition to AI data centers in the US, where concerns over electricity costs, water consumption and environmental impacts emerged as issues in November’s midterm elections.

Ahead of the elections, a September poll from the University of Massachusetts Amherst found that 65% of Americans opposed the construction of AI data centers in their communities, with just 11% expressing support. Opposition crossed party lines, with 76% of Democrats and 52% of Republicans opposing local construction.

During the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which saw Democrats win control of Congress, voters backed limits on data center development in 40 of 41 local contests tracked by Ballotpedia. The measures included outright bans, temporary moratoriums on new projects and requirements for voter approval of large-scale developments.

#4809. Nvidia agrees to $290M settlement over crypto mining revenue disclosures

The proposed settlement would resolve a shareholder lawsuit dating back to 2018 that alleged Nvidia misled investors about its exposure to the cryptocurrency industry.

Nvidia has agreed to pay $290 million to settle a shareholder lawsuit dating back to 2018 that alleged the chipmaker misled investors about the extent to which cryptocurrency mining drove its gaming revenue, according to a Tuesday court filing.

The proposed settlement, which requires court approval, covers investors who purchased or otherwise acquired Nvidia common stock between Aug. 10, 2017 and Nov. 15, 2018, and suffered qualifying losses.

The lawsuit was initially filed by a US ironworkers’ union-affiliated fund, with Swedish asset manager Öhman Fonder and Dutch pension fund PGB later appointed as lead plaintiffs. Investors alleged that Nvidia misrepresented the source of demand for its gaming graphics processing units (GPUs).

During the 2017–2018 crypto boom, miners purchased Nvidia’s GeForce GPUs to mine cryptocurrencies, with sales recorded as gaming revenue. An analysis commissioned by the plaintiffs estimated that Nvidia understated its crypto-related GPU sales by $1.1 billion between May 2017 and July 2018.

In November 2018, Nvidia lowered its quarterly revenue forecast amid weakening mining demand. Its stock fell 28.5% over the following two trading sessions, according to the plaintiffs. Nvidia disputed the allegations, arguing that it could not reliably quantify the impact of cryptocurrency mining demand on its gaming revenue.

The case was dismissed in 2021 before a federal appeals court revived claims against Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang in 2023. The US Supreme Court dismissed its review of the case without ruling on the merits in December 2024, and the case was certified as a class action in March 2026.

The settlement represents approximately 14% of the total damages claimed by investors, according to the plaintiffs’ attorneys, who intend to seek up to 21.4% of the settlement fund in legal fees.

A hearing on the proposed settlement’s preliminary approval is scheduled for Feb. 4, 2027.

#4805. US inflation rises to 3.8% ahead of December Fed meeting, clouding crypto outlook

US core inflation rose more than expected in October as markets anticipate a December interest rate hike, which could slow a crypto market recovery.

US inflation picked up in October, adding pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its upcoming December meeting and potentially complicating a recovery in cryptocurrency markets.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index – the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation – rose 3.8% from a year earlier, in line with economists’ expectations, according to Wednesday’s report from the US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA).

Core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, rose to 3.3% annually from 3.1% in September, its highest level in nearly three years and above economists’ expectations of 3.2%. On a monthly basis, both measures of inflation rose 0.3%.

“October’s PCE report shows that inflation is not yet under control as much as markets had hoped,” Salman Parcy, managing partner of Cequire Capital, said in comments shared with Cointelegraph.

The report comes just two weeks before the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting. With inflation still above the central bank’s 2% target, investors are concerned that further interest rate hikes could make it harder for the crypto market to recover.

The data comes as total crypto market capitalization has fallen about 32% since the start of the year, from around $3.09 trillion on Jan. 1 to $2.09 trillion on Wednesday, according to CoinGecko.

Related: Hot US inflation raises odds of half-point Fed hike in December

As of 4:01 p.m. UTC on Nov. 25, traders were pricing in a 94.4% chance that the Fed would raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point in December, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. Such a move would bring the Fed’s benchmark interest rate to a range of 4% to 4.25%.

Meanwhile, separate GDP data released Wednesday showed that the US economy grew at an annualized rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, up from an earlier estimate of 3.4%. With consumers and businesses spending more, the Fed could have more room to raise interest rates to fight inflation without causing a sharp economic slowdown.

While markets widely expect a December rate hike, Fed officials have taken different views on how the central bank should tackle inflation. Fed Governor Christopher Waller, for instance, has suggested raising rates by a quarter of a percentage point in both December and January or by half a percentage point in December alone.

New York Fed President John Williams, however, has called for a more cautious approach, saying last week that the situation does not call for “dramatic action,” according to Yahoo Finance.

The Fed will make its December rate decision before the next PCE inflation report, which is scheduled for Dec. 23.

Experts explained that if the Fed raises interest rates, borrowing could become more expensive, and investors may favor lower-risk investments, such as US government bonds, over cryptocurrencies.

With inflation still high, the Fed also has less room to lower interest rates, while further rate hikes could reduce the amount of money flowing into crypto markets, Parcy explained. “While it is still not a major bearish signal for crypto, it does make a near-term recovery harder,” he said.

However, Parcy noted that a return of institutional investment and improvements in the broader economy could help the crypto market recover.

Ryan Kirkley, co-founder and CEO of Global Settlement Network (GSN), said Bitcoin (BTC) and technology stocks face similar challenges as investors deal with higher borrowing costs.

“I still see Bitcoin and tech stocks trading on the same liquidity cycle, so as long as borrowing costs stay elevated, I’d expect both to remain under pressure,” Kirkley said in comments shared with Cointelegraph.

For now, all eyes will be on the Fed’s December meeting, when the central bank will also share its latest forecasts to give investors a better idea of what’s to come.

#4803. Ethereum Foundation backs Keccak-256 to counter quantum, AI threats

Ethlabs co-founder Julian Ma told Cointelegraph that AI poses a more immediate threat as Ethereum prepares for one of its biggest security overhauls since the Merge.

The Ethereum Foundation has recommended the Keccak-256 hash function as the basis for Ethereum’s cryptographic defenses against quantum computing and AI-assisted attacks, according to a blog post on Nov. 24. It chose the nearly 20-year-old function over Poseidon, a newer alternative the team had spent years attempting to harden.

Described by Ethlabs co-founder Julian Ma as “one of the largest efforts done in blockchain, not just in Ethereum,” the planned switch to hash-based cryptography acts as a critical move to protect the chain from the future threat of quantum-based attacks.

Keccak-256 is a cryptographic hash function that converts data into a fixed-length, 256-bit digital fingerprint used to verify data integrity, while quantum attacks use quantum computing to exploit weaknesses in existing cryptographic systems.

The chosen hash function would form the backbone of Ethereum’s post-quantum security, meaning that “if it is broken, everything else is broken,” the blog post said. With nearly two decades of resistance to attacks, Keccak was considered the most secure of the candidates evaluated by the Foundation.

While quantum resistance is the long-term goal of the switch, protecting against the rising threat of AI-assisted attacks has become a more immediate priority.

The initial focus of the Ethereum Foundation’s research on hash functions was balancing the speed and security of the new system. The Foundation passed on SHA-256, despite its use in Bitcoin, citing collision attacks affecting more than half of the hash function’s protection.

Since the research began, the performance of SNARKs, cryptographic proofs that allow statements to be verified without showing the underlying data, has improved. The Foundation noted that security was therefore “the deciding factor.”

Related: Ethereum Foundation doubles protocol security team ahead of overhaul

Poseidon, the hash function the team had previously focused on, was designed in 2019 specifically to handle zero-knowledge proofs. Traditional hashes like SHA-256, used by Bitcoin, made these proofs painfully slow. However, reduced-round versions of Poseidon were still open to attacks, and improvements in SNARK performance reduced its speed advantage.

Two other functions also considered by the foundation were BLAKE2 and BLAKE3, general-purpose hashes used in VPNs and the Linux kernel. While their speed was noted in the blog post, limited research into their resistance to attacks led the Foundation to rule them out as options for the Ethereum network.

Although the move to hash-based cryptography is focused on reducing the threat of quantum computing, AI has become a primary security concern. Increasingly powerful AI systems have raised concerns about the security of cryptographic systems, including those Ethereum relies on.

Ethlabs’ Ma, who proposed an approach to post-quantum and post-AI resistance on Ethereum on Nov. 11, told Cointelegraph that although post-quantum security is important, “AI is here today and it’s breaking everything around us.” He noted that in this environment, “Ethereum has kept 100% uptime, basically because it has a culture of being extremely proactive on these security issues and prioritizing security over everything else.” In the blog post, the Foundation noted that Keccak-256 had so far remained unaffected by AI-assisted attacks.

Ma explained that much of the Ethereum community is aligned on making post-quantum security a priority. He said nearly all core developers are keen to put it first, which he described as “80, 90% of the win,” with the remaining discussions centered on which other upgrades should make way for it.

For the teams that build Ethereum’s software, the Foundation noted that the choice of Keccak would require little new code. Ethereum has used Keccak for its addresses since launch, so client teams can reuse existing code instead of building and testing a new hash from scratch. The Foundation also recommended that the consensus layer, which currently relies on SHA-256, gradually move over to Keccak for certain hashing operations.

Core developers have not approved the Ethlabs proposal, and the Foundation’s published roadmap still targets December 2029 for quantum resistance.

#4800. Why ECB collateral eligibility could boost demand for tokenized bonds

Past ECB decisions offer clues to the value of using bonds as collateral, while US derivatives exchanges face a different calculation over their Bitcoin holdings.

The European Central Bank (ECB) plans to expand the range of tokenized bonds banks can use as collateral to borrow cash, a move that could lower borrowing costs for issuers and give bond funds additional ways to earn securities-lending fees.

For a borrower preparing a bond sale, the choice of where to issue it could affect the interest bill. From June 2027, the ECB plans to accept qualifying bonds issued on platforms licensed under the EU’s distributed ledger technology pilot regime.

A bank that buys one could raise cash from the Eurosystem using the bond as collateral without selling it. That flexibility may be worth a higher bid at the sale.

Historical bond prices offer a clue to the potential impact. A study of 160 changes in Eurosystem collateral eligibility found that yields on newly eligible corporate bonds fell by 4.6 to 20 basis points relative to bonds still waiting to qualify.

Demand to borrow eligible securities also rose, according to the study. A bond fund could earn a fee by lending the security to a bank that wants to pledge it as collateral. Luxembourg’s 1.7 billion euro ($1.86 billion) tokenized bond already qualified through an earlier route.

Banks bought 47% of the October issue, close to their 51% share of Luxembourg’s conventional 10-year sale in March. Those figures show banks were willing buyers in both markets. As eligibility expands, the more revealing figures will be the yields banks accept on newly eligible debt and how much of it they actually pledge.

#4799. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’: Inside the Psychedelic 1970s-Inspired Dystopian Sets

Francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins. Before bringing a new installment of her bestselling dystopian saga to the big screen, the two join forces to envision how the fictional world of Panem will take shape. “I go to New York each time, and we sit in a conference room at Scholastic,” says Lawrence, who has directed five of the franchise’s six films. “We go through the book page by page and beat out what we think the movie is going to look like.”

Lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena. Set twenty-four years before the original The Hunger Games (2012) plotline, the prequel follows District 12’s sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada)—the future mentor (played by Woody Harrelson) to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson)—as he is selected to fight in the Second Quarter Quell, a particularly sadistic rendition of the Games held every twenty-five years.

District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.

Though the dystopia is set in a future North America, the previous prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023), drew from the architecture of 1940s and ’50s postwar Berlin to depict evil President Snow’s rise to tyranny. Set forty years later, Sunrise explores Panem at a new stage of its evolution. Designed by returning production designer Uli Hanisch, the film follows Haymitch from his impoverished mining district, which barely evolves throughout the series’s sixty-five year timeline, to the opulent Capitol, whose extravagance is expressed through a 1970s-inflected visual lexicon.

“I realized the ’70s fall right smack in the middle between that movie and the originals, so we could lean into that,” says Lawrence. Hanisch and his team incorporated references to Andy Warhol, Studio 54, and the decade’s psychedelic color palette, appropriating its progressive spirit to convey the Capitol’s opulence and authoritarianism—and, particularly in the arena, using the aesthetic as a means of deception. “To turn the ’70s style from something progressive, liberal, young, and open-minded into something evil is a twist,” says Hanisch. “But that is the key to the entire film’s design.”

Haymitch and Maysilee as allies in the arena. The forest portion was filmed separately near Cologne, Germany.

The stylistic choice is also a poignant nod to Collins’s original inspiration for the book series. The 1970s marked a transformation in American television: as color TVs became ubiquitous in households across the country, sporting spectacles, variety shows, and beauty pageants flourished, establishing cultural touchstones that would help shape the contemporary reality programming Collins critiques and satirizes in The Hunger Games. “I was flipping through the channels one night between reality television programs and actual footage of the Iraq War, when the idea came to me,” Collins recalled in a 2018 interview with The New York Times. The juxtaposition inspired her to explore just-war theory for young people through an authoritarian dystopia in which mass entertainment is an instrument of political control.

From an abandoned rural steel mill to authoritarian monuments from postwar Berlin, the film draws on politically charged German sites to capture Panem at a pivotal stage in its political and architectural evolution.

Production Designer Uli Hanisch at the District 12 set. “District 12 is the most sentimental set to me because I’d known this site near my hometown my entire life,” Hanisch says.

To recreate the Appalachian-inspired, deteriorating industrial landscape of District 12 that was shot in Atlanta in the original series, the production utilized a sprawling abandoned steel mill in Duisburg, Germany, Hanisch’s hometown. “I wish we had it in the original movies, because it is an unbelievable space,” Lawrence says of the post-industrial, rural landscape, which also appeared in The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, Hanisch’s first film in the franchise. “Everywhere you look is exactly how I have always imagined District 12.”

While District 12 was filmed near Atlanta in the original films, director Francis Lawrence’s fascination with German architecture brought production to Berlin for The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. It was there that he began collaborating with Berlin-based production designer Hanisch, who proposed this steel mill nearby his hometown for the new location. Upon seeing photographs, Lawrence exclaimed, “Are you kidding me? ... Let’s go tomorrow,” and promptly flew out to see it for himself.

The production designer added modest huts at the edge of a nearby quarry to recreate the Seam, home to Haymitch, his girlfriend Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak), and fellow tribute Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), its humble dwellings contrasting the more prosperous merchant district inhabited by fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace).

“Unlike the Capitol, District 12 doesn't evolve stylistically throughout the films. Nobody is investing in it, and everything is gradually deteriorating,” Hanisch explains. The vivid purples and oranges of the Capitol’s ‘70s palette are notably absent, only appearing prominently in propaganda decorating the reaping square, including Hunger Games campaign materials and posters portraying Snow as Panem’s number-one Peacekeeper.

Druscilla in the Capitol before the tribute interviews, which is broadcast to all of Panem.

In the Capitol, however, the architecture takes on a distinctly ‘70s flair. Rooted in the Roman concept of panem et circenses, or “bread and circuses,” from which Panem takes its name, the architecture reinforces the government’s manipulation through spectacle. In the background is Berlin's International Congress Centrum, a colossal, aluminum-clad convention center that opened in 1979, which Lawrence describes as “Cold War-era Berlin showing off in a modern way.” As West Berlin’s most expensive postwar building, the futuristic complex was publicly subsidised to showcase economic prosperity and technological advancement—an evocative backdrop for the Capitol’s own display of authoritarianism.

“It’s a time of peace for the Capitol with no rebel attacks, so Snow's had time to build the city up in a way that is an extravagant show of power,” Lawrence explains. The chariot parade, which introduces the tributes before the Games, similarly unfolds against the historically-charged Berlin Olympiastadion, which was designed by Werner March for the 1936 Olympics under Nazi Germany to project state power and an illusion of timeless permanence.

The upstairs library in Plutarch’s home, which he inherited from the Heavensbee dynasty. Reflecting the Capitol’s classic style, it contrasts the Plutarch’s modern downstairs salon which features Warhol-inspired portraits, including one of director Lawrence.

The Capitol's grandeur is also exhibited inside the mansion of Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), a cameraman with historic ties to Panem’s ruling class. “This was one of my favorite sets because of the scope and scale” Lawrence says, noting how its excess reflects the dynasty's immense wealth. Filmed at Berlin's late-1960s modernist Congress Center, the circular residence required twenty-five vans of retro-modern furniture to fill it. The salon, decked in vibrant 1970s furnishings and Warhol-inspired art, showcases Plutarch's modern sensibilities, in stark contrast to the upstairs library inherited from his family. “We wanted to distinguish Plutarch from the dynasty he comes from,” Lawrence explains, reflecting on how the expansive volumes must be a facade of intellectual sophistication.

The set decoration department spent weeks hand-folding and assembling thousands of hollow cardboard books, interspersed with real volumes, including a collection of Edgar Allan Poe’s poetry, which Plutarch references to Haymitch. “We imagined Plutarch might actually be the first Heavensbee to read some of those books,” Hanisch says. “He even says the library is one of the few worthwhile things his ancestors accomplished.”

The library's custom-built curved bookshelves envelope the characters, symbolising the insularity of Capitol society. “Circles represent both inclusion and exclusion,” Hanisch says. “If you are in the circle, you're in. And if you're not, you're out.” As fans of the franchise will know, Plutarch (originally played by Philip Seymour Hoffman) later reveals himself as a double agent and leader of the underground rebellion against Snow’s regime.

The aspect ratio expands as Haymitch ascends into the eye-shaped arena, emphasizing the landscape’s immersive scale and beauty. While scouting locations, Lawrence drew inspiration from the dramatic landscapes in Terrence Malick’s A Hidden Life. “I had that in my head, only it was a little trippier. The Asturias were perfect,” he recalls. The kaleidoscopic design also inspired the official logo of the 50th Hunger Games, extending the arena’s psychedelic imagery into the Capitol’s propaganda.

The Quarter Quell arena, in particular, embodies the surreal, fantastical ethos of the 1970s that permeates the film, illustrating how the Capitol exploits beauty to disguise its underlying manipulation and brutality. “As I was reading with Suzanne, I said there was an Alice in Wonderland-like element to it, which made me think of the song ‘White Rabbit,’ which made me think of the late ’60s, early ’70s,” Lawrence recalls. “That kind of broke something open for me.”

Designed in the shape of an eye, the eight to ten mile arena serves as a metaphor for the Capitol's omnipresent surveillance. A golden Cornucopia forms its pupil; vibrant meadows its iris; and the surrounding mountain ranges its whites. In the book, Haymitch describes the especially lethal arena masquerading as an idyllic landscape as a “poisonous beauty of an arena.”

Lawrence and Haymitch in the arena. The physical flowers were concentrated in the foreground, while visual effects extended the colorful landscape into the distance

Seeking to capture as much natural landscape as possible, Hanisch and location manager Klaus große Darrelmann discovered a remote valley in Asturias, Spain, surrounded by the Cantabrian Mountains. Transforming the isolated valley into a psychedelic paradise proved an enormous undertaking.“The arena was our nemesis,” says Hanisch, recalling how the production had to bring extensive resources to the remote terrain. “You can't even imagine how far away it was or how hard it was to get to.” Crews spent weeks individually installing hundreds of thousands of artificial flowers throughout the meadows and forests.

Despite the arena’s dreamlike beauty, water sources, flowers, and vegetation conceal deadly poisons. “It’s the most colorful and playful dystopia you’ll ever see,” producer Nina Jacobson says. Perhaps more than anywhere else in Panem, the arena encapsulates how the Capitol weaponizes the electric zeitgeist of the ‘70s as an instrument of control. “To have something so overwhelmingly beautiful and seductive but poisonous and deadly is very cruel,” Hanisch says. “That contradiction captures the mentality of Panem at this point in its history.”

#4798. In the Berkshires, an Intensely Yellow Kitchen Is Anything but Mellow in This Lakeside Cottage

“I personally would not want this yellow in my kitchen,” says Jess Cooney. It’s a cheeky comment about the beaming hue she herself chose for clients in the Berkshires—a color that defines their entire lakeside home, one she calls the diva of the whole project, requiring (no, demanding) decisions in every square foot to balance out its intensity.

Cooney’s clients didn’t blink at the bold idea. Unusually carefree for a couple with high-powered jobs, they gave the AD PRO Directory designer free license to create. The bungalow was purchased as a weekend retreat from life in New York, but even before paint swatches were discussed, the kitchen was a sticking point. “The kitchen was crazy—it was this tiny little makeshift kitchen,” says Cooney.

Cooney’s clients weren’t initially convinced by reclaimed brick flooring in the entryway, but Cooney’s team proved convincing—they believed the space needed a worn palette to counterbalance the intensely yellow kitchen. Much to their clients’ delight, it worked beautifully. A Croft House Morro Credenza with leather-front doors anchors the space, topped with a vintage lamp from Millerton Antiques Center and set beneath an unknown artwork from Brimfield Flea Market.

Cooney opted to stain wood-paneled walls in custom blue and brown stains from Rubio Monocoat, allowing rustic grains to shine through. Atop a Jaipur Hazan rug, an upholstered George Smith Emma Ottoman anchors the room and is accompanied by a set of armchairs and a velvet mordoré sofa from Lawson-Fenning. A 20th-century oil painting by Paul Berg hangs above the reworked fireplace, while in the corner, above a Charles Dudouyt side table, hangs a vintage painting sourced from The Little Store in Massachusetts.

“We just decided to kind of lean into it and go almost in a maximalist way,” says Cooney of the dining room’s focal point, a painting by K.G. Narendra Babu that inspired the home’s many colors. For the inside of a Four Hands Camila Sideboard, they commissioned artisan Joel Haynes to hand-paint a leafy pattern. A Hubbardton Forge Disq fixture hangs above a custom Bossi dining table surrounded with Tribute Modern Dining Chairs from Craft Associates.

The husband, an English lawyer, craved a small cabin in the woods, while the wife, an Italian who loves cooking, wanted a home large enough to host intimate gatherings. “This house was a happy compromise,” says the husband. But while the home spans three levels and around 4,500 square feet, the main floor measured just about 1,000. The kitchen, in a cramped corner, didn’t cut it

Cooney’s team reconfigured a few walls. They collapsed oversized closets in the entryway, shrinking the space to a slimmer mudroom while letting the entire layout exhale, expanding the footprint of the semi-open cooking area. The room is now the proper heart of the home, and its bright yellow cabinets aren’t shy about it.

Cabinets with glass windows were fabricated by Westek Architectural Woodworking and feature an array of white porcelain that punctuates and calms the intensely painted millwork; the pieces were all sourced from shops in the Berkshires, including Millerton Antiques, All that Jazz, and Montage Antiques.

“It’s the diva of the project,” says Cooney of the yellow Benjamin Moore paint used throughout the kitchen, a choice that influenced nearly all palettes throughout the home. Ceilings, walls, and upper cabinets were painted in Farrow & Ball’s New White.

The kitchen island is topped with a wooden counter and is paired with Amber Interiors Cade Counter Stools in walnut. A set of Matthew Fairbank Allegro Pendants hang above the island.

The saturated hue, Benjamin Moore’s Glen Ridge Gold, wasn’t a choice made on a whim. Like many colors peppering the home, it was inspired by a painting by Chennai-based artist K.G. Narendra Babu that now hangs in the couple’s dining room. The artwork was given to the couple by a family member who worked in India, and it features an array of folk and musical motifs.

“The whole point of the project is that it’s bright and energetic and deeply relaxing at the same time,” says Cooney. “That was the trust that they put in us—to believe that both could happen.”

The architecture itself lacked a definitive style. Light traces of Arts & Crafts style gave Cooney a point of view to reinvent existing character. A fireplace in the living room is now reimagined with glazed brick Clé tiles, their dappled surface cladding the surround with clean lines and a crafted look; a custom stain allowed wood-paneled walls to bear rustic grains but in modern blue-green tones.

To expand the kitchen’s footprint, Cooney reclaimed space from unnecessarily large closets in the entryway. Her team moved the wall to install smaller, but equally useful, cabinets that turn the space into a mudroom. The custom millwork, crafted by Westek Architectural Woodworking and painted in Farrow & Ball’s Blue Gray, complements a vintage rug and a built-in bench.

A custom walnut vanity injects warmth as an alternative to a colder stone. Cooney’s team used a boat sealer to coat and protect the walnut, giving the material a high-gloss finish. A fabric shade made with Eric Kuster’s Micha 002 textile occupies the space that might traditionally feature a mirror. “You can kind of break a rule and have it be playful and fun, especially in a powder bath,” says Cooney, noting that a mirror hangs on the side wall instead. The wallcovering is Pierre Frey’s Uberon print.

Cooney describes an almost cottagey feel in the primary, thanks to a walnut Flora Bed by Jacob May, which was locally made and turned by hand, layered with cozy and textural textiles like Parachute Home’s Hand Stitched Cotton Quilt. Gentle patterns add to the mix through a Scandinavian kilim with geometric design from Rug & Kilim, and light drapes made with a Best Buds textile by Kerry Joyce.

Making the most of existing features, light touches to the bathroom reimagined the space, like painting existing wainscoting in Farrow & Ball’s Tanner’s Brown, and covering the walls in a botanical House of Hackney Herbarium wallpaper. For a touch of texture, Cooney also layered vintage rugs and set an antique Victorian bamboo chair in the corner below the window.

With a view over the living room, Cooney says the lofted floor is like a little escape within the small cottage. Leaning into the cozy feel, the team went with a layered look. A brass chest anchors the space, paired with a black armchair owned by the clients, which was reupholstered with a burgundy fabric from Abraham Moon & Sons, and a Lawson-Fenning Morro Sectional in a linen blend.

The clients’ only real hesitation was a bit of a surprise: the reclaimed brick Cooney specified for the mudroom. It is laid in a herringbone pattern with colors that appeared to shift across the surface. That yellow kitchen? Totally fine. But the expressive bricks? Too dramatic. “We relied on the team’s judgement, and this feature is now one of our most favorite parts of the home,” says the husband, noting how guests often compliment the mudroom.

“I feel like this house is kind of us unchecked,” says Cooney of her clients’ trust. “No one checked us, so we were allowed to do the fullest extent of what we wanted to do.” Her clients could easily have staged their own diva moment after the cabinets were painted in screaming yellow, before everything else around it fell into place around it; but they let the vision come into full focus.

As if cantilevered over the hill, a screened-in porch is the best of both worlds. “You don’t have to have everything be indoor-outdoor in a covered porch—you can really pull the inside out there and not worry so much,” says Cooney, nodding to choices like Henning Kjaernulf dining chairs from the 1960s purchased from Lone Fox. And while most might use a lighter color in this space, Cooney chose a deeper Farrow & Ball Hopper Head paint for the walls and window frames, which she says helps punctuate the view in a beautiful way.
